items.title: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages?
items.summary: Models refuse harmful requests more when told they are being tested, with a 14.4‑percentage‑point increase in Indic languages and a rise in benign refusals from 6.9% to 11.3%.
items.why: It shows safety tests in Indic languages may not reflect real‑world model behavior.
items.desc: Large language models (LLMs) can often tell when they are being tested. This ability, known as evaluation awareness, can lead models to act more cautiously during safety evaluations than in real use. Existing work has studied evaluation awareness almost entirely in English, although models serve users in many languages. Indic languages are spoken by over a billion people, yet evaluation awareness remains almost entirely unstudied in them. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English. A set of cues varies whether the model is told that it is monitored and whether the monitoring is a safety test. Models refuse harmful requests more often when they are told that they are being tested. This increase appears in all four models and all six languages. items.title: Twice Upon a Time: Complementary Representations for Time-Series Reasoning
items.summary: A dual‑view model combining line plots and normalized delay embeddings improves TSRBench accuracy over single‑view baselines.
items.why: It shows that complementary visual representations can boost time‑series reasoning in language models.
items.desc: Time Series Language Models (TSLMs) enable language-based understanding and reasoning over temporal data, yet a fundamental question remains: what information should their time-series representations preserve, and what variation should they factor out? Existing TSLMs typically expose the language model to a single representation, imposing a fixed inductive bias across downstream tasks. We instead introduce complementary representations as a design principle for time-series reasoning. Our model combines two visual views: line plots preserve absolute measurements and the observed coordinate frame, while normalized delay embeddings factor out positive amplitude rescaling and offsets while exposing temporal structure. Dedicated visual encoders integrate both views into a shared language model through visual tokens and multi-level feature fusion. Evaluation-time interventions verify that the two views exhibit distinct invariance profiles, while single-view ablations show that their combination is particularly beneficial beyond basic perception, with the large gains in prediction and reasoning. items.title: Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas
items.summary: A trained 8B model outperforms Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT‑6 Astra on a contamination‑free benchmark for generating diverse scientific ideas.
items.why: It shows set‑level reinforcement learning can improve diversity and quality of LLM‑generated scientific ideas, useful for research pipelines.
items.desc: One of the first steps of a research pipeline is generating ideas. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate this step, but most of this work optimizes the quality of individual ideas, while overlooking diversity. In our work, we study document-grounded ideation, focusing on increasing the diversity of LLM generated ideas and ensuring they are high quality. Given prior papers, a model must propose a set of ideas that are each high-quality and clearly distinct from one another, while also being grounded in the input documents. To optimize for this, we propose training with a set-level reinforcement learning objective. In our setup, in a single generation, the model writes K structured idea cards grounded in the source papers, and the set is scored jointly, where each idea's quality is weighted by its distance from the ideas written before it. This teaches the model to steer each new idea away from its predecessors. items.why: It offers a new way to generate and analyze humanoid policies, potentially speeding up deployment and understanding of robot control networks.
items.desc: Recent advances in robot learning have driven rapid progress in humanoid control, enabling increasingly agile behaviors in the real world. However, humanoid control networks are typically obtained through conventional training procedures, while comparatively little attention has been given to directly modeling the distribution of their learned weights and generating functional networks in weight space. In this work, we investigate whether high-performing humanoid control networks can be generatively modeled directly through their weights. We adopt a latent diffusion framework that couples a linear autoencoder with a Diffusion Transformer. The autoencoder compresses actor network parameters into a compact latent space, and the Diffusion Transformer models the distribution of these latents. Trained on networks collected from reinforcement learning for the Unitree G1 robot, our approach generates deployable networks that perform various motions in the real world, including walking, dancing, and spin kick. items.title: Hierarchical Residual Policy Learning for Real-World Mobile Manipulation with Sparse Human Guidance
items.summary: The paper introduces HiRe-MoMa, a hierarchical residual framework that fine‑tunes a frozen base policy for mobile manipulation, achieving stable, sample‑efficient real‑world performance with sparse human guidance.
items.why: It demonstrates how to efficiently adapt complex robotic systems with limited human input.
items.desc: Mobile Manipulation (MoMa) is a cornerstone of autonomous robotic systems, yet real-world fine-tuning remains a formidable challenge because of high-dimensional action spaces and intricate coupling between heterogeneous modules. In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa (Hierarchical Residual Mobile Manipulation), a systematic framework for stable and sample-efficient real-world fine-tuning of complex MoMa systems. At its core, HiRe-MoMa adopts a Hierarchical Residual Architecture that fine-tunes a frozen base policy. A Policy-Agnostic Residual learns additive corrections atop the base policy, while Hierarchical Decoupling splits the residual into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning, mitigating gradient interference and aligning corrections with the platform's physical hierarchy. To improve sample efficiency in data-expensive real-world settings, we propose Expert-Guided Value Alignment, which leverages sparse human interventions with under 20% training coverage to reshape the critic's value landscape, effectively guiding autonomous exploration through expert priors. items.title: Co-Evolving Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents
items.summary: The paper proposes a method that jointly trains language agents to generate and forecast multi‑step action sequences, enabling acting and forecasting to co‑evolve without extra inference cost.
items.why: It improves sample efficiency and learning from intermediate steps in language agent training.
items.desc: Training language agents is bottlenecked by the high cost of long-horizon rollouts, yet standard agentic reinforcement learning (RL) learns only from a terminal scalar reward, leaving the supervision in intermediate steps largely unused. Prior work exploits this supervision through value targets that estimate per-step success probabilities or observation targets that fit environment response. Both are hard to construct well: (1) value targets come from the same single scalar signal for each step in the trajectory, and (2) observation targets, such as web pages and terminal logs, are long and noisy and reach only one step ahead. We propose \name, which adds a third kind of multi-step action targets. On successful on-policy trajectories, \name trains the policy backbone to generate the action sequences that follows each history. Each action is also supervised when forecast from the preceding histories, forming a temporal ensemble that the shared backbone absorbs during training, and this enables acting and forecasting to co-evolve. items.title: Your Transformer Is Secretly Elastic
items.summary: A retraining‑free method that elastifies pre‑trained transformers into a single model that adapts across computational budgets by jointly ranking MLP neurons and attention heads, achieving smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity.
items.why: It allows efficient deployment on heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads without costly retraining.
items.desc: Scaling up transformers has produced models with broad capabilities, deployed across heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads. Yet, model families offer only a few fixed sizes (e.g., S, B, L), forcing users to commit to a model based on hardware and latency constraints. This rigidity is often suboptimal under varying query loads. We introduce a retraining-free method that elastifies pre-trained transformers into a single model that adapts on-the-fly across a continuum of computational budgets. Our key contribution is a differentiable relaxation of the functional unit-ranking problem: unlike prior work, which optimizes a single importance weight per MLP block or attention head, we rank every individual MLP neuron and attention head jointly, on a common scale, by minimizing the model's loss under soft pruning across many sparsity targets, all at once. Across 27 vision and text transformer encoders ranging from 22M to 8B parameters, our method yields smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity and outperforms one-shot baselines under deep pruning. items.title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
items.summary: The paper shows that competition among bidders in first-price auctions for AI prompts reduces the price of anarchy.
items.why: It indicates first-price auctions can allocate AI prompts efficiently, reducing welfare loss.
items.desc: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). items.title: Continuum Attention
items.summary: Continuum Attention replaces discrete key/value lookup with continuous integration over a memory curve, improving validation negative log likelihood over softmax and focal attention.
items.why: It could improve Transformer performance.
items.desc: We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), a causal Transformer attention operator that replaces discrete key and value lookup with integration over a continuous, piecewise linear memory curve. Each query induces an exponential relevance density along the curve. Integrating the density and interpolated values yields exact normalized attention from closed form exponential moments, including half token boundary contributions. The gradients follow analytically from moments of order at most two, enabling parallel GPU implementations while retaining quadratic sequence complexity and the standard Transformer decoder. Compared with ordinary softmax and focal attention, CA reduces mean validation negative log likelihood by 0.0200 and 0.0480 nats per byte, respectively, winning all paired comparisons. An additional disjoint validation slice yields a 0.0457 nats per byte advantage over the strongest selected softmax baseline, with a paired 95% confidence interval. These findings motivate continuous integration as a promising attention alternative while leaving larger scale generalization open.

items.title: Latent Compaction with Test‑Time Training
items.summary: A method that compresses key–value caches via test‑time training achieves 96.7% accuracy on RULER at 32× compression, far outperforming baseline KVZip+.
items.why: It enables efficient long‑context inference without retraining the model.
items.desc: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. items.title: One Task, Many Interfaces: Simple Cross-Interface Consistency Training Improves LLM Agent Robustness
items.summary: Cross‑Interface Policy Regularization (CIPR) improves LLM agent robustness by penalizing KL divergence between action distributions across two interfaces, recovering 10.5 % of accuracy lost to interface perturbations while preserving performance on the unchanged interface.
items.why: It demonstrates a simple self‑supervised method to make LLM agents resilient to interface changes, important for deploying agents in varied environments.
items.desc: Post-training binds the competence of an LLM agent to the interface it was trained on. Semantics-preserving perturbations of that interface, such as renaming an action or changing the notation, leave the underlying task unchanged yet make the agent worse at it. Scoring each sample independently means interface randomization only broadens this dependence from a single interface to the training interface distribution, so out-of-distribution perturbations still degrade the agent. We propose Cross-Interface Policy Regularization (CIPR), a self-supervised objective that replaces action names with uninformative identifiers and presents each training sample under two interfaces in which equivalent actions are identified by construction. CIPR penalizes the KL divergence between the action distributions induced under the two interfaces, so the policy behaves consistently across them. We evaluate CIPR in both supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training, where it improves robustness. On agentic function calling, held-out interface perturbations reduce the accuracy of a post-trained agent by nearly 25%, and CIPR recovers 10.5% while leaving accuracy on the unchanged interface intact.

items.title: Manacá-1B-Instruct-2: Reproducible Safety Alignment for a Native Brazilian-Portuguese LLM. Negative DPO Results, a Controlled Composition Scan, and a Silent Failure Mode of the LLM Judge
items.summary: Manacá-1B-Instruct-2, a 1.72B‑parameter Brazilian Portuguese LLM, was released with safety alignment via SFT, achieving a safety lower bound of 94.1% that exceeds four baseline models.
items.why: It provides a safety‑aligned open‑source LLM for Brazilian Portuguese, filling a language gap in open‑source AI.
items.desc: Brazilian Portuguese remains underserved by open-source language models, and the few that are safety-aligned rarely document what did not work or validate comparisons with statistical significance. We present Manacá-1B-Instruct-2, the second-generation post-training alignment of Manacá-1B (1.72B parameters, trained from scratch for PT-BR), with an SFT corpus of 291,223 examples. We document three DPO attempts, all negative, including a case where the training reward margin reaches 1.0 while free generation does not change at all, and show that safety came from a dedicated safety-SFT (LLM-jp AnswerCarefully style), refined over three iterations until closing the safety-helpfulness frontier. A controlled scan of the fraction of general data in the safety-SFT mix (10% to 60%) reveals a non-monotonic over-refusal curve with a knee point at 40-50%. The final model is compared against four external PT-BR models on the same items, with Wilson confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction: the lower bound of its safety interval (94.1%) lies above the upper bound of all four baselines. items.title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
items.summary: Periodic forgetting of search state in agent teams boosts discovery performance by up to 39% over a single-agent baseline.
items.why: It shows that managing memory can accelerate automated research.
items.desc: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further. We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. items.title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios
items.summary: The study shows that larger LLMs perform better overall, with the top model slightly outperforming humans on behavioral persuasion but still trailing humans on cognitive inference.
items.why: It highlights limits of current LLMs in social reasoning and informs design of more socially intelligent agents.
items.desc: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.

items.title: PrismaCoder: Pushing the Boundaries of Open Multimodal Code Intelligence through Decomposed Rubric Synthesis
items.summary: PrismaCoder presents an open multimodal code intelligence framework that uses a rubric‑based data pipeline to curate training data and guide reinforcement learning.
items.why: It provides a systematic way to improve data quality for multimodal code models, enabling higher‑quality open‑source outputs.
items.desc: Multimodal code intelligence connects the symbolic world of programs with the visual world their execution creates. Interest in this capability is burgeoning, as models are increasingly asked to produce charts, webpages, animations, and semi-structured documents. Recently, proprietary models have pushed far ahead, producing interactive artifacts even from a text description or a screenshot alone. Yet their data and training remain closed, and open progress is held back by the quantity and quality of available data and by the pipelines and methods for producing it. Quality is the harder of the two, since a sample must be correct as a program, well built, and above all visually right once rendered. No existing signal covers all three. Execution often returns just a pass or fail, code similarity does not map to the visual output, and task-specific verifiers do not generalize. To push open progress further, we start from the data side with PrismaForge, a hierarchical data pipeline centered on a synthesized rubric that decomposes these factors into checkable criteria. items.title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
items.summary: ChunkAct reduces LLM calls by 2.9× and improves task success by 5.0 points on LIBERO‑Pro by executing chained primitives as a single chunk.
items.why: It makes agentic robotics more efficient by cutting LLM reasoning overhead.
items.desc: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. items.title: Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards
items.summary: Tev-Gym introduces 1,170 verified long‑horizon task environments with dense, progressive rewards, using a latent‑world-first approach and progress‑potential reward shaping to improve agent training.
items.why: It provides a scalable, verifiable dataset and reward‑shaping method that makes training long‑horizon agents more efficient.
items.desc: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. items.title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning
items.summary: A training‑free decoding method shortens chain‑of‑thought reasoning by 31% for Qwen3‑32B while keeping accuracy unchanged.
items.why: It cuts inference cost without sacrificing performance.
items.desc: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. items.title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
items.summary: Hybrid Reasoning Agents combine latent internal reasoning with text-based tool interactions to enable transparent, tool-integrated agentic behavior.
items.why: It demonstrates a new architecture that improves agent transparency and tool use.
items.desc: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. items.title: The Last Remote Sensing Model Built by Humans? Casting Any Earth Observation Task as Recursive Self-Improvement
items.summary: An autonomous coding agent built Earth observation models that beat state‑of‑the‑art performance on four benchmarks while using only about 1 % of the training labels.
items.why: It shows that AI agents can automate model creation for remote sensing, reducing human effort and label costs.
items.desc: Earth observation (EO) models are still built by hand. For each new task, experts design a training recipe and tune it against a benchmark. We show that this loop can be handed to an agent. Any verifiable task can be cast as a harness and a verifier, where the harness defines what the agent may use and the verifier defines what counts as success. Every EO task can be made verifiable, through labeled benchmarks, independent sensors, physical models or the repeated observation of the same place. Given only these two components, a general-purpose coding agent builds the EO model and improves it recursively on its own outputs. Settings long treated as separate research problems, from learning with a handful of labels to adapting across domains, become choices of harness and verifier. On four EO benchmarks spanning optical, SAR and multispectral time-series imagery, agent-built models surpass the state of the art and keep most of that accuracy from about 1% of the training labels. This establishes a new paradigm for EO, in which people design harnesses and verifiers and agents build the models, so EO models improve as agents do.

items.title: APTree: Extended Behavior Trees for Adaptive and Scalable Automated Robotic Task Planning in Construction
items.summary: APTree automatically generates modular task plans for construction robots by coordinating multiple symbolic planners at runtime.
items.why: It enables scalable, automated task planning for construction robotics.
items.desc: Task planning for robots in off-site construction prefabrication is primarily manual, leading to planning inefficiencies and reluctance to adopt robotic solutions. Existing approaches provide limited support for scalable, modular automated task planning and localized runtime replanning. This paper proposes APTree, a model-driven framework that integrates automated task planning with modular task execution using behavior trees as the execution model. APTree repeatedly applies and coordinates heterogeneous symbolic planners to automatically generate and compose modular task plans at runtime. To support this approach, we develop a domain-specific language for the formal specification and validation of task plans, together with a compatible execution engine. We evaluate APTree on the real-world livMatS Biomimetic Shell pavilion, where it models the construction robotic fabrication domain, detects injected specification and planning errors at design time and runtime, and automatically generates large-scale task plans by coordinating three symbolic planners across numerous planning modules. A machine-checked formal analysis further shows that composed execution and local replanning are s

items.title: Lost in Implicit Routing: How LLM Agents Fail to Load Relevant Skills at Scale
items.summary: Adding 1,000 irrelevant skills to a library drops LLM agents’ skill‑loading recall from 73.6% to 27.4% and raises zero‑load rate from 9.3% to 51.6%.
items.why: It demonstrates that implicit skill routing becomes unreliable as skill libraries grow, harming agent scalability.
items.desc: Reusable skills let LLM agents load task-specific instructions on demand, but they make execution depend on implicit routing over skill metadata. We test whether this design scales by holding SkillsBench tasks and their golden skills fixed while adding irrelevant skills. We find skill routing collapse: agents increasingly load fewer or no skills, even though the relevant skills remain available. With 1,000 irrelevant skills, loaded-skill recall falls from 73.6% to 27.4% and the zero-load rate rises from 9.3% to 51.6%, whereas explicit selection from the same library retains 73.9% recall. Loading other skills, including plausible alternatives to golden skills, is too rare to explain this decline. Masking only the descriptions of irrelevant skills largely restores skill loading, yet with the metadata intact, explicitly asking agents to plan skill use still yields lower recall than preselection. These findings point to semantic interference from descriptions and instruction interference when skill choice competes with task execution. We also evaluate explicit preselection as a practical mitigation, including its coverage and latency trade-offs. Our analysis informs skill protocols and

items.title: The Geometry of Language Model Logits: Generic Structure and Learned Departures
items.summary: Ordered vocabulary logits follow a log-linear relation z_(r) ≈ μ – α log r, with trained models showing α≈1.4–1.7, higher than the initialization baseline α≈0.2, and α correlates with predictive performance.
items.why: It shows that language models learn a distinct logit geometry beyond generic extreme‑value effects, informing decoding strategies and model evaluation.
items.desc: Autoregressive language models produce, at every prediction step, a vocabulary-sized logit vector whose structure determines the conditional next-token distribution. We empirically identify that the ordered vocabulary-head logits follow a remarkably consistent log-linear relation \[ z_{(r)} \approx μ- α\log r. \] across prediction contexts, architectures, and scales, emerging progressively during pretraining. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic analysis of the logit geometry underlying the distributional assumptions used in the prior decoding work. While controlled order-statistic baselines spanning bounded, light-tailed, and heavier-tailed distributions can largely explain the observed log-linear geometry, they do not explain the systematic shift in the slope $α$: trained language models exhibit $α\approx 1.4$--$1.7$, sitting well above the initialization baseline ($α\approx 0.2$) . Moreover, $α$ correlates with predictive performance, suggesting that it captures learned structure beyond generic extreme-value effects.

items.title: A Global View of How LLMs Value Human Time
items.summary: The paper finds that LLMs recommend higher compensation for delayed appointments in Europe, lower in Africa, and underestimate time value in Asia and South America relative to GDP per capita.
items.why: It reveals that LLMs embed geographic biases that could affect fairness in AI assistant services.
items.desc: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as personal assistants; however, little is known about how they capture national-level preferences on a global scale. Given that "time" is a universal and representative concept, we examine LLMs' time preferences by varying only users' country and measuring the compensation LLMs deem appropriate for a 60-minute appointment delay. We then compare LLMs' responses with GDP per capita on Purchasing Power Parity (GDP_PPP), Mean Income, and a literature-based index (Patience Score). Our results across 193 countries and 5 LLMs demonstrate that people's time across the world is evaluated in noticeably different ways among LLMs, as well as varying levels of robustness under prompt variations. LLMs consistently recommend the highest compensation for Europe, but mostly the lowest for Africa. Based on GDP_PPP, LLMs underestimate the value of time for users living in Asia and South America. These findings indicate that geographical patterns are embedded in LLMs and may translate in different treatment in agentic settings.

items.title: The Smart Buildings Challenge: Learning Foundation Models for Real-World Optimization at Scale
items.summary: A challenge is proposed to develop building foundation models that adapt to new buildings with minimal configuration, enabling scalable building optimization.
items.why: It could enable AI-driven climate impact by scaling building optimization globally.
items.desc: Buildings cause nearly 40\% of carbon emissions in the US. Of total building emissions, HVAC systems are responsible for approximately 40-60\% and account for 15\% of global energy consumption. Despite advances in artificial intelligence, most buildings still operate as inefficiently as they did decades ago. Building optimization, perhaps more so than any other optimization problem, has enormous potential for Machine Learning (ML) driven impact on climate change, in both the short and long term. One of the biggest obstacles for building optimization is the lack of policy transfer. Most building control systems, whether simulation or learning based, don't generalize: they only work well for the building they were developed for, but not for other buildings. items.title: EgoOmniWorld: Unifying Egocentric Understanding via Ego-Action-World Interactions
items.summary: The paper introduces EgoOmniWorld, a benchmark of 24,166 egocentric video QA groups organized around node, edge, chain, and loop interaction structures.
items.why: It provides a structured benchmark for egocentric video understanding, enabling systematic study of multimodal interactions.
items.desc: Egocentric video understanding spans diverse capabilities, modalities, and evaluation formats, yet these are often studied in isolation despite their tight coupling in real-world interaction. We propose the Ego-Action-World interaction loop as a unifying principle: the wearer perceives the world, forms goals, acts, changes the world, and uses feedback to guide subsequent behavior. Based on this view, we introduce EgoOmniWorld, a benchmark organized around four complementary interaction structures: Node captures ego, action, and world states; Edge captures directed relations among them; Chain captures linked dependencies; and Loop captures feedback-closed interactions. We develop an interaction-first, evidence-grounded data pipeline that extracts structured interactions from egocentric videos, grounds them in visual and auditory evidence, and generates questions according to their interaction structure. Required modalities and single- or multi-turn formats follow naturally from the supporting evidence and dependencies. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. items.title: Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?
items.summary: A benchmark testing LLMs on graph navigation using the Wikipedia Game found that leading models achieved human-comparable success but did not significantly outperform humans across languages and domains.
items.why: It introduces a standardized, API-independent benchmark to evaluate how effectively language models navigate large multi-step document and citation networks.
items.desc: Language models increasingly support or automate information retrieval from document collections too large to index. This task is difficult when it requires specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge. We used the Wikipedia Game to test language models on an analogous information retrieval task. In the game, players must reach a target article using only article links. We compared sentence embedding models and LLMs across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-literature datasets. We construct very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and of paper citations using OpenAlex and provide code to build and navigate them. This allows the study of language models' navigation capabilities without relying on third-party APIs. We compared the models with human and TF-IDF benchmarks. The Wikipedia Game format enables robust comparisons across techniques, languages, and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, although the best models (GPT-o3 mini, GPT-4o, QwQ:32B, and DeepSeek-R1:70B) achieved comparable success. Performance and rankings varied across languages and topics, with implications for practitioners utilising these techniques.

items.title: Hide and Seek: HIDE Concepts to SEEK Explanations for Black Box Models
items.summary: Researchers introduced Hide and Seek (HnS), a concept-based attribution method for black-box vision models that requires neither access to model weights nor labeled concept datasets.
items.why: It enables image-level explainability for proprietary or closed-weight vision models by using vision-language models to locate and mask concepts.
items.desc: Interpreting machine learning model predictions is a central challenge, particularly for black-box vision models. Concept-based attribution methods interpret models using human-understandable concepts. Existing concept-based methods can only interpret classification and regression models. They require access to model weights or large concept-annotated datasets, and most methods cannot provide image-level attribution. We propose Hide and Seek (HnS), a new method for concept-level attribution that does not require access to model weights or labeled concept datasets. HnS can interpret a wide range of vision models. Given a concept and image set, HnS retrieves concept-aligned images using a vision-language model, localizes the concept within each image, masks the localized region, and measures attribution from the change in the black-box model's output between the original and masked images. This enables faithful attribution by directly measuring the model's behavior and supporting local attributions. We validated HnS on CelebA and COCO-Stuff. Compared to existing methods, HnS showed better agreement with ground-truth attributions. We demonstrated the applicability of HnS on diverse ta

items.title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
items.summary: Researchers introduced RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework that uses predictive world models to iteratively guide action selection and drive recursive policy self-improvement across coding, GUI, and scientific tasks.
items.why: It demonstrates a viable path for AI agents to continuously self-improve across diverse domains without relying solely on expensive external feedback.
items.desc: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world-model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. We introduce RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on JEPA-Anything that uses predictive world models to guide action and learning-data selection. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world-model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks govern the retention of updated policy-model pairs. Across diverse computational and scientific domains, RSI-Anything demonstrates substantial gains. In code repair, with the coder fixed, success increases from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% through predictive selection and 31.2% after world-model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Graphical user interface (GUI) evaluations showed higher task completion, while average actions decrease by 39.4%. Across five successive policy versions, laboratory-planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01%. items.title: When VLMs Destroy What They Know: Spatial Representations Fall Below Lexical Priors
items.summary: Researchers find that vision-language models identify spatial relations at local tokens but lose that information when aggregating text into global representations such as EOS tokens or mean pooling.
items.why: It uncovers a systematic representational bottleneck in VLMs that degrades spatial and relational reasoning even when models perform well on standard output evaluations.
items.desc: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly analyze and reason about images, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations faithfully encode the structured relations required for such reasoning. We introduce EICS (Evaluation-Invariant Concept Stability), a metric for testing whether representations consistently encode concepts under controlled one-concept interventions, and CASP-VL (Causally controlled Spatial Perturbations for Vision-Language models), a benchmark of causally controlled spatial perturbations derived from Visual Genome scene graphs. Across multiple VLM architectures, we find that spatial relations are represented substantially less faithfully than lexical information, even when the same models score well above chance on compositional benchmarks. Further analysis shows that the relation is identifiable at the predicate's own tokens but is lost when the sentence is aggregated into a global representation, whether through the (EOS) token or by mean pooling. These findings reveal a systematic failure invisible to output-based evaluation: VLMs do not preserve, in the representation used downstream, relational information that is present in their own input.

items.title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping
items.summary: A systematic benchmark of tabular deep regression objectives reveals that quantile loss consistently outperforms standard MSE baselines, while global early stopping inherently limits performance across regions with varying noise.
items.why: It provides practical guidance for training deep tabular models and exposes a fundamental drawback of standard early-stopping strategies in heteroskedastic settings.
items.desc: While deep learning models for tabular data have recently received significant research attention, the choice of objective functions for regression tasks remains an understudied degree of freedom. Several lines of research offer alternatives to the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE), but differences in datasets, backbones, and evaluation protocols make their practical benefits difficult to compare. In this work, we address this gap by performing a systematic re-evaluation of regression objectives across a broad collection of established tabular datasets and multiple neural backbones. Our comparison reveals that many proposed objectives provide limited or inconsistent gains over a properly tuned MSE baseline, while quantile loss yields consistent aggregate improvements over MSE across the tested backbones. We then identify a limitation that remains even with this strong objective: regions with different levels of target noise can reach their best predictive performance at different training epochs. Consequently, a single global early-stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions, even when the objective can represent heteroskedastic target distributions. Mot

items.title: Structural Automata for Neural Semantic Parsing
items.summary: Researchers introduced accepting-path decoding using structural automata to guarantee valid semantic representations within length limits, significantly improving Smatch++ scores on DRS and AMR parsing.
items.why: It solves a key failure mode in constrained generation where token-by-token masking can leave models with valid prefixes that cannot be properly completed within budget limits.
items.desc: Neural semantic parsers generate meaning representations token by token, yet well-formedness depends on references, scope, and graph relations that unfold during generation. Constrained decoding prevents locally invalid tokens but does not guarantee that a valid prefix can be completed within a fixed output-length limit. We investigate structural automata at three stages of DRS parsing (decoding, post hoc processing, and training) and additionally evaluate decoding on AMR. For decoding, we introduce accepting-path decoding (APD), which maintains a verified completion within the remaining length limit and follows the model's preferred token whenever that token can also be completed. APD guarantees an accepted output without retracting tokens. Under tight length limits, it improves Smatch++ over local masking by 5.1 and 2.4 points on DRS and by 6.4 and 3.2 points on AMR, comparable to rollback under the same limit, which retracts tokens. items.desc: Large language models reuse the same attention heads across tasks, but identifying these shared heads does not explain what they do differently in each task. A natural source of inspiration is task-dependent interactions among shared brain regions, which motivate a network view of language-model computation. We measure how interventions affect attention heads and the activation state in later layers (influence), as well as the answer (importance). items.title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
items.summary: Researchers introduced RATED, an agent tool retrieval framework combining semantic search with contextual bandits to dynamically adapt to real-time API outages without model retraining.
items.why: It addresses a critical production failure mode for autonomous agents by dynamically routing around failing external tools with negligible latency.
items.desc: As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED (Reliability-Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent, a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query-tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. items.title: X-AgentRed: Red-Teaming Personal Agents in Evolving Multi-Service Ecosystems
items.summary: Researchers introduced X-AgentRed, a self-evolving red-teaming framework that uses tool dependency graphs and execution feedback to discover harmful cross-service tool call paths in personal agents.
items.why: It addresses a critical blind spot in agent safety by systematically uncovering unintended harmful outcomes arising from complex, multi-service tool interactions.
items.desc: Personal agents increasingly connect to services across the web and applications by using tools. As the effects of their actions accumulate and interact across services, unintended or harmful outcomes can arise when agents fulfill benign user requests. Proactively identifying these compositional failures requires systematically exploring diverse cross-service paths. Existing red-teaming methods often simply prompt LLMs to identify potentially harmful paths from task and environment descriptions or decompose harmful objectives specified by humans or LLMs into seemingly benign action combinations. However, generation is biased toward patterns learned during training, potentially favoring familiar tool combinations and leaving novel cross-service interactions underexplored. To address this, we propose X-AgentRed, a self-evolving red-teaming framework that discovers harmful tool call paths through a graph of tool dependencies and expands and refines them using execution feedback. items.title: Studying Comics at Scale with Artificial Intelligence: The PAGE Framework and Three Studies of American Comics and Japanese Manga
items.summary: Researchers released PAGE, an AI framework that parses comic scans into panels, text, and metadata, enabling large‑scale analysis of 3,929 American comics and 87 manga volumes.
items.why: It demonstrates how AI can transform humanities research by scaling analysis of visual and textual media.
items.desc: Comics are one of the great visual records of the twentieth century: hundreds of thousands of pages in which a mass readership saw its leaders, its wars and its heroes. Most of this record has never been studied as a whole; comics scholarship proceeds one book at a time. We argue that artificial intelligence, including generative models, can change this to the benefit of the medium itself. We propose PAGE, a framework that makes artificial intelligence an instrument for comics research. It parses every scan into panels, text and a bibliographic record; annotates each page with a vision-language model that follows a written codebook, as a human coder would; grounds samples of these readings in human annotation; and explains change across an archive, with estimates controlled for publisher and genre. We demonstrate the framework on 3,929 American comic books (1938--1956) and 87 volumes of Japanese manga, in three studies, each resting on a different capability. items.title: OpenPA: Forced-alignment-free Multi-granular Pronunciation Assessment with Mixed-transcript Adaptation
items.summary: OpenPA uses Whisper's cross-attention to predict word- and utterance-level pronunciation scores without forced alignment, achieving best performance on speechocean762 and zero-shot on MultiPA.
items.why: It enables practical, alignment-free pronunciation assessment across response settings.
items.desc: Recent advances in automatic pronunciation assessment (APA) have driven a shift from scripted to free-form assessment. However, existing methods often rely on multi-stage pipelines with forced alignment and separate feature extractors, limiting their practicality across response settings. In light of this, we propose OpenPA, a novel APA framework that leverages Whisper's cross-attention mechanism to jointly predict word- and utterance-level pronunciation scores without forced alignment. Through mixed-transcript adaptation and adaptive substitution weighting, OpenPA accommodates heterogeneous transcripts across closed- and open-response settings within a single model. Trained solely on speechocean762, OpenPA achieves the strongest overall performance among evaluated systems under in-domain closed and simulated open-response conditions, while maintaining its performance zero-shot on MultiPA. An additional cross-task evaluation on oral-cancer speech suggests its potential applicability beyond non-native speech.

items.title: On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons---a statistical look at the METR plot
items.summary: The paper finds that AI time horizons are nearly flat between 2–30 minutes, making a 10× jump from 3 to 30 minutes easier than from 30 minutes to 5 hours, and offers improved estimates and diagnostic plots.
items.why: It helps benchmark AI progress in interpretable units and guides the design of realistic time‑horizon tests.
items.desc: METR's 50\% time horizon measures the human completion time of software tasks that an AI solves with 50\% probability, allowing AI capabilities to be expressed in interpretable units. On 228 tasks and 26 AIs, we recompute the time horizons using splines and item-response theory to relax the assumption that the AI difficulty of a task depends linearly on the log of human time. Our fitted spline can be interpreted as a function that \emph{converts} human time to AI difficulty; it is nearly flat in a region from 2--30 min but close to linear elsewhere. Hence, a time-horizon jump from 3 min to 30 min is much easier than one from 30 min to 5 hours despite the same multiplier of $10 \times$. Overall, we contribute time-horizon point estimates that perform better under a cross-validated suite of proper scoring rules, as well as diagnostic plots for assessing time horizons' construct validity. We suggest that time horizons be interpreted together with the diagnostic plots, especially as new time-horizon-based benchmarks are proposed or existing ones grow to include longer tasks.

items.title: From Reactive Containment to Proactive Assurance: Lessons from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Agent Security Incidents
items.summary: The paper shows that AI agents can reach real systems outside their authorized test scope, demonstrating the need for proactive security assurance.
items.why: It highlights that agent security incidents can breach boundaries, requiring verification during operation.
items.desc: In 2026, cybersecurity evaluations involving OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google agents reached real systems outside their authorized test scope. The paths were different. OpenAI agents exploited research infrastructure, coordinated across runs, and compromised parts of Hugging Face's production environment. Anthropic reported cases in which a misconfigured third-party environment exposed real systems to agents pursuing simulated cyber tasks. In a separately reported evaluation, Google's Gemini accessed three real organizations through an unintended internet route; Google stated that the model stopped in all three instances. Taken together, the cases show why an evaluation cannot rely on an assumed boundary. That boundary must be verified while the agent is operating. This comparative instrumental case study develops a Proactive Agent Security Assurance Cycle (PASAC) and a five-layer Boundary Assurance Stack. The framework combines risk-tiered task design, executable scope contracts, pre-run validation, least-capability access, independent egress enforcement, credential restrictions, cross-run monitoring, automatic stop conditions, and evidence-based reauthorization. items.title: BrickBench: Evaluating Agentic Brick Design

items.why: It offers a testbed for AI agents to design physically buildable LEGO assemblies.
items.desc: We propose BrickBench, a benchmark for agentic text-conditioned LEGO-set design. Given a prompt, an agent is tasked with producing an assembly that not only satisfies semantic and design criteria, but that can also be physically built. To do so, it must select parts from a discrete library and reason jointly about local and global constraints. We score validity, alignment, and design across three settings that vary in scale and part availability. We provide BrickAgent, an environment for coding agents to construct, inspect, and validate their designs. We find that leading agents largely satisfy verifiable physical and semantic requirements, but fall short of human designs. We release our benchmark and environment at http://www.brickben.ch

items.title: Bi-FORK: Generative Modeling of High-Dimensional Bifurcating Systems
items.summary: Bi-FORK learns one-to-many solution maps for high-dimensional bifurcating systems, generating complete trajectories and recovering distinct solution branches in a single amortized pass.
items.why: It enables generative modeling of complex physical systems with bifurcations, which prior methods could not handle.
items.desc: Bifurcations are ubiquitous in physical systems, from structural buckling to fluid and climate dynamics, yet they remain largely unexplored in deep learning. At a symmetry-breaking bifurcation, a single input admits multiple equally valid solutions, violating the one-to-one assumption underlying most learned physical surrogates. We introduce Bi-FORK, a generative framework for learning these one-to-many solution maps in high-dimensional systems. Bi-FORK generates complete trajectories through latent flow matching, preserving space and time coherence, and uses repulsion-guided sampling to recover distinct solution branches in a single amortized pass. We evaluate Bi-FORK on buckling beams, mechanical metamaterials, and Allen-Cahn phase separation, spanning continuous, discrete, and field-valued bifurcations with discretizations up to 260,000 points. Bi-FORK recovers the multimodal solution structure while scaling several orders of magnitude beyond prior approaches, opening generative modeling to high-dimensional bifurcating physical systems.

items.title: Caught in the Act: Probes Effectively Detect Sabotage and Catch Unverbalized Deception
items.summary: White‑box probes trained on the largest deception dataset reach up to 99.7% AUC in detecting hidden goals, outperforming existing text‑monitoring baselines.
items.why: It demonstrates a scalable approach to detect deception in large language models, enhancing safety monitoring.
items.desc: Recent incidents have highlighted the challenge of monitoring LLM agents and the danger of models deceiving people. We show that white-box deception detection via probes can be scaled up to frontier monitoring settings by collecting the largest deception dataset to date for training probes and introducing a novel probe architecture which can aggregate information across many layers and tokens. Our probes achieve 98.8% AUC in SHADE-Arena, surpassing an Opus 5.5 text-monitoring baseline, and show improved efficacy as the underlying model is scaled up. To push our probes to their limit, we test them on several cases where deception cannot be determined from the context alone. In these cases, which we refer to as introspective deception, the ground truth can only be determined through careful elicitation or thorough knowledge of a model's training data. In one such evaluation, we show that probes can distinguish transcripts containing a model's true hidden goal from other goals with an AUC of up to 99.7%. items.title: Ecology of AI Agents: Collaboration Creates a Population Threshold for Takeoff
items.summary: Collaboration among AI agents lowers the population threshold for a self‑reinforcing takeoff, increasing the risk of misaligned agent proliferation.
items.why: It shows how agent collaboration can accelerate dangerous population growth.
items.desc: AI agents can now conduct real-world cyberattacks, scale up capabilities with the number of agents, and collectively pursue misaligned goals to obtain rewards. Together, these factors raise the risk of a population explosion of misaligned agents: agents could compromise computers and secretly deploy additional agents, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where larger populations develop greater collective cyber capability and expand further. This raises a fundamental question: What determines whether a population of misaligned agents remains contained or takes off into this self-reinforcing cycle? This population-level problem is ecological safety: unlike individual-agent or multi-agent safety with a fixed population, it concerns the dynamics of the population itself. Here, we develop an ecological theory of AI-agent populations based on a population growth equation in which fitness (growth rate) depends on cybersecurity capability. We show that, without collaboration, the population takes off only when individual-agent capability exceeds a critical threshold. items.title: FastBench: Can Streaming VLMs Perceive High-Dynamic Real-World Streams?
items.summary: FastBench benchmark shows streaming VLMs struggle with high-dynamic real-world video, with the best model scoring only 50.7%.
items.why: It highlights current limits of streaming VLMs for real-time video understanding.
items.desc: Streaming Video Large Language Models (VLMs) enable continuous video understanding, yet existing benchmarks focus on low-dynamic scenarios. Under bounded context budgets, models must balance temporal history, spatial resolution, and temporal granularity; sparse sampling at 1--2 FPS misses fast events. We introduce FastBench to evaluate high-dynamic perception in real-world video streams. Its trajectory-grounded pipeline combines QA generation from high-FPS clips, filtering of questions answerable at 2 FPS, answer verification using SAM3 and CoTracker3 trajectories, and three rounds of human inspection. FastBench contains 306 QA pairs across eight domains, six capabilities, and forward, instant, and backward temporal scopes, with human-annotated evidence intervals. We also present ProactiveFrame, a training-free baseline that adjusts incoming frame rates through text tokens. A dual-tier sliding window retains recent high-FPS observations while downsampling older ones into sparse history. items.title: WOVEN: Weaving Visual World Modeling into Multimodal LLMs
items.summary: WOVEN is a new benchmark and training source for visual transition reasoning that improves multimodal LLMs' performance.
items.why: It helps close the gap between models and humans in spatial and temporal reasoning.
items.desc: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) struggle with spatial, embodied, physical, and temporal reasoning. We hypothesize that these failures reflect a shared deficit in visual transition reasoning, and test whether this capability can serve as a shared training primitive, one that different models can learn from different supervision sources and reuse across different tasks, with a systematic training recipe. Existing benchmarks document these deficits separately but do not support controlled comparisons across scenes, actions, and reasoning operations. We therefore introduce WOVEN, a training source and benchmark for visual transition reasoning that organizes transition supervision by scene, action, and reasoning type, using diverse, realistic rollouts from video-pretrained generative models: 36,076 examples across 20 scene types, 5 action types, and 8 reasoning types. We first evaluate 38 frontier MLLMs (e.g., GPT-5.4 and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B) and find a substantial and systematic deficit: even the strongest models fall far below humans, and the failures recur across model families and persist with scale. items.title: Predicting Alignment Generalization with Value Representations
items.summary: Activations-based representations predict alignment generalization better than textual descriptions, achieving a correlation of 0.45 versus 0.05.
items.why: It offers a method to anticipate how fine‑tuning on one value influences other values, aiding safer alignment.
items.desc: LLM developers post-train their models to exhibit prosocial values and behavioral traits, which are enumerated in an alignment target. However, while recent post-training developments have yielded models that score highly on alignment evaluations, training models on sets of narrow behaviors still influences their behavior across unseen contexts and environments in unexpected ways. In this paper, we establish the task of alignment generalization prediction, i.e., predicting how fine-tuning a model to follow a given value changes its behavior across a wide range of held-out values. We conduct a large-scale analysis of alignment generalization effects across 66 values found in modern alignment targets, and benchmark representational techniques on the alignment generalization prediction task. We find that representations based on model activations when applying values in context significantly outperform methods based on textual descriptions of the values. Specifically, the best activations-based methods achieve correlations of 0.45 with our generalization matrix, compared with 0.05 from description-based baselines. items.title: ViSkill: Reinforcing VLM Agents with Evolving Visual‑Native Skills
items.summary: ViSkill encodes successful interactions as visual skill cards that improve VLM agent performance, achieving a 0.91 success rate on Sokoban, FrozenLake, and PrimitiveSkill with cold‑start initialization.
items.why: It demonstrates a closed‑loop skill learning framework that boosts sample efficiency and convergence speed for visual‑language agents.
items.desc: Skill-augmented agents improve sample efficiency by distilling successful trajectories into reusable strategies. Yet most existing approaches remain text-centric, linearizing spatial layouts and action-state correspondences into language that loses critical geometric structure. Recent efforts have begun incorporating visual evidence, but construct and update skills separately from policy optimization, leaving their mutual improvement underexplored. We propose ViSkill, a visual-native skill learning framework that encodes successful interactions as composite visual skill cards directly accessible to VLM agents. Retrieved skills guide both inference and reward shaping, while successful trajectories are distilled back into the library, forming a closed feedback loop in which skill accumulation and policy improvement reinforce each other. An optional cold-start mechanism further accelerates early-stage learning. Evaluated on Sokoban, FrozenLake, and PrimitiveSkill, ViSkill achieves an overall success rate of 0.89, rising to 0.91 with cold-start initialization, outperforming all evaluated proprietary and open-source baselines while converging faster than standard PPO. items.title: SpaceCast-Bench: Evaluating Predictive Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
items.summary: SpaceCast-Bench introduces a benchmark for predictive spatial reasoning, showing that the best model scores only 58% versus 87% human performance.
items.why: It highlights a gap in current vision-language models' ability to predict unseen spatial outcomes.
items.desc: Existing spatial reasoning benchmarks mainly test spatial perception: reading off relations already visible in the input. Yet real-world spatial intelligence demands predictive spatial reasoning: constructing a scene from observations, anticipating how an intervention changes it, and reasoning about the unseen outcome. We introduce SpaceCast-Bench, the first benchmark to directly and diagnostically evaluate this capability. Built around an observe-transform-infer framework, its 3,862 questions from 182 real-world scenes span 16 task types at three levels: static perception, local prediction, and global prediction, progressively requiring scene understanding, spatial state updating, and relational inference over unobserved outcomes. Evaluating 21 models exposes a stark gap: the strongest model reaches only 58.0% against 87.2% human performance, while spatially specialized models remain near random chance. Controlled analyses further reveal that bridge views are critical for integrating distributed observations, and that explicit 3D evidence benefits models more reliably than generated outcome images or videos. items.title: Long Text to Predictive Features: LLM-Guided Blockwise Feature Engineering via Executable Program Search
items.summary: LLM-BlockFE builds offline executable feature programs from long text, eliminating runtime LLM calls for risk‑control predictions.
items.why: It reduces inference cost while preserving LLM insights.
items.desc: Industrial risk-control systems typically rely on structured-data models for efficient prediction, yet substantial valuable information remains embedded in unstructured long text. Extracting this information through manual feature engineering is labor-intensive, while requiring a large language model (LLM) to process every real-time input may not meet practical deployment requirements. To address this challenge, we propose LLM-BlockFE, an LLM-guided offline feature construction framework that converts long text into executable feature programs, thereby avoiding LLM calls during online inference. LLM-BlockFE constructs feature programs by incrementally appending immutable code blocks and evaluates candidate features using a downstream model. items.title: Never Look Back: Understanding Persistence in 3D Object Memory from Egocentric Videos
items.summary: Researchers introduced Ledger, a persistent 3D object memory system that tracks object locations, histories, and contextual descriptions from egocentric videos. Ledger improves HD‑EPIC accuracy from 29.7% to 42.6%, UCS‑Bench accuracy from 33.8% to 38.5%, and localizes Ego4D objects with a 0.99 m median error.
items.why: It advances the ability of embodied assistants to remember and recall objects over time, improving spatial reasoning.
items.desc: As we move through the world and carry out everyday tasks, we encounter objects that may become relevant only later. We are capable of recalling where we left something or what was inside a container, even without knowing we would need it later. Here, we study how an embodied assistant can build a similar memory from egocentric videos, by observing a person's day-to-day activities. We present Ledger, a persistent 3D object memory that combines object locations, their histories, and contextual descriptions. It associates observations across the recording and retains objects after they leave the view, including those the person never touches. It clusters each object's observations by resting locations and records a move only after repeated evidence, reducing the effect of localization noise. Short descriptions preserve details such as an object's contents or supporting surface. It saves these records to later answer spatial questions without having to access the original images or video. Our memory raises HD-EPIC accuracy from 29.7% to 42.6%, UCS-Bench accuracy from 33.8% to 38.5% and localizes Ego4D objects with a 0.99 m median error on returned predictions. items.title: Decoupling Exploration from Optimization in RLVR
items.summary: The paper introduces Exploration‑Distillation (ExpDis), a framework that separates exploration with a novelty bonus from optimization. Explorer policies generate novel trajectories, which are filtered for correctness and distilled into a student policy trained without the novelty bonus, leading to better performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks compared to DAPO.
items.why: It demonstrates a method to enhance model reasoning capabilities while preserving quality, a key challenge in reinforcement‑learning‑based language model fine‑tuning.
items.desc: Modern language models undergo reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) on top of already-trained checkpoints. A key promise of RLVR is the discovery of new reasoning strategies. In principle, a model can sample novel ideas absent from its prior training data. In practice, however, augmenting RLVR with strong novelty incentives has seen limited success and can degrade model quality. Because verifiable rewards supervise only a narrow slice of the model's knowledge and behavior, such degradations are difficult to recover from. Instead, we decouple exploration from optimization in a framework we call Exploration-Distillation (ExpDis). We train one or more explorer policies with a novelty bonus in the reward, filter their trajectories for correctness and quality, and distill them into a separate student policy. The student policy is then trained without a novelty bonus. We repeat the above procedure for several rounds, alternating between exploration and optimization. This decoupling allows us to aggressively scale exploration without degrading the student policy. items.title: EngramEdit: Decoupled Knowledge Updates in LLMs through Conditional Memory
items.summary: EngramEdit proposes a method to update factual knowledge in large language models by computing target memory representations for multiple expressions of a fact and jointly adjusting shared n‑gram embeddings. The approach penalizes frequent embeddings to preserve unrelated knowledge, enabling independent updates while keeping the Transformer backbone unchanged.
items.why: It offers a practical way to refresh LLM knowledge without full model retraining.
items.desc: Conditional memory architectures such as DeepSeek Engram use input n-grams to look up learned embeddings, expanding the capacity of large language models (LLMs) with limited additional computation. Beyond model scaling, this architecture has demonstrated the potential to decouple factual knowledge storage from general-purpose computation, offering a promising route to updating factual knowledge while keeping the Transformer backbone fixed. Realizing this potential is challenging because different expressions of a fact may activate different n-gram embeddings, while updating shared embeddings can unintentionally change the model's predictions about other facts. We propose EngramEdit for decoupled knowledge updates through conditional memory. EngramEdit first computes target memory representations that make the model predict the updated fact across multiple expressions. It then jointly updates the shared n-gram embeddings to match these targets across expressions and edits, penalizing updates to frequently reused embeddings more strongly to preserve unrelated knowledge. items.title: Long-WAM: Scaling the Context of World-Action Models
items.summary: The paper presents Long‑WAM, a framework that scales the visual context for causal world‑action models in real‑time robot control. By pretraining a video foundation autoregressively and preserving the history‑to‑future structure, the authors show that extending context from 0 to 19.2 seconds raises success rates on RoboCasa GR‑1 from 63.3 % to 78.7 % and achieves top performance on LIBERO‑Long, RoboTwin 2.0, and DOMINO, while enabling deployment on RTX 5090, DGX Spark, and Jetson AGX Thor.
items.why: It demonstrates that longer visual histories and autoregressive pretraining can substantially improve autonomous robotic performance, informing future robot‑control system design.
items.desc: Real-time robot control demands enough visual history to infer motion and task progress, but processing that history can delay action. We present Long-WAM, a model-system framework for scaling the context of causal world-action models under real-time control constraints. Our central finding is that access to history is not the same as using it: longer histories pay off far more when the video foundation is pretrained autoregressively (AR). We first learn causal prediction from robot and egocentric videos without action labels, then preserve this history-to-future structure during world-action adaptation. On RoboCasa GR-1, increasing context from 0.0 to 19.2 seconds raises success from 63.3% to 78.7%, whereas a bidirectionally pretrained initialization shows no net gain; robot-domain AR pretraining further raises peak success on GR-1 and LIBERO-Long. Long-WAM also achieves the best results among compared methods on LIBERO-Long, RoboTwin 2.0, and DOMINO.
